The extension is to several predictors, which the chapter now reaches in "Adding a second predictor." -->

In this, our final chapter, we'll introduce the last inferential procedure that we will cover: the regression technique. This is an extension of the idea of correlations among variables, much like ANOVA extends our ability to analyze differences among groups beyond what the $t$ test is capable of. And as we'll see, regression is actually a variation of the ANOVA technique itself.

## Recap: correlation

<!-- PLAN: this recap could shrink to a few sentences; the table repeats Chapter 17's. -->

First, let's quickly recap the gist of the correlation statistic. Pearson's $r$ correlation coefficient quantifies the strength of the linear relationship between two variables. I find the easiest way to think about this is to imagine or sketch an ellipse around all the points on your scatterplot. For a correlation of zero or a very weak correlation, the ellipse will basically be a circle. As the value of Pearson's $r$ increases, the circle becomes a tighter and tighter ellipse, until for a correlation of one, you can put a straight line through all the points.

Here's the little example dataset we used in the previous chapter, showing scores on two variables for seven people: how much coffee they drank on the morning of an exam and how they did on the test.

| Participant | Coffee (cups) | Test score |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 75 |

: The coffee and test score data from the correlation chapter. $r = -.50$. {#tbl-coffee-scores-again}

<!-- FIX: "They just look correlated here by chance" affirms the null. We failed to reject it; we didn't show the correlation is zero. -->

With just seven points on the scatterplot, it's difficult to see, but the ellipse around the points would be something like this. It was a strong correlation, but with so few scores in the data, it was not statistically significant in our hypothesis test. We couldn't reject the null hypothesis that scores came from a population in which the two variables have a correlation of zero. They just look correlated here by chance.

{{< interactive-figure coffeeEllipseScatter makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,90],[0.5,60],[0.5,85],[1,65],[1.5,50],[1.5,65],[2,75]],"xLabel":"Coffee (cups)","yLabel":"Test score","xDomain":[0,2.5],"yDomain":[40,100],"showEllipse":true,"ellipseScale":1.7,"showR":true,"controls":false,"maxWidth":"30rem"}' fallback="The coffee and test score scatterplot with a downward-sloping ellipse traced around the seven points, illustrating the correlation of r = −.50." >}}

## The line of best fit

<!-- FIX: the last sentence of this paragraph runs on ("This is in contrast to ... where regression here shows"). The idea is one of the best in the chapter; it could be sharpened with Chapter 4's fact that the mean minimizes squared deviations: the regression line is a mean that's allowed to tilt. -->

So now let's talk about regression. Basically, rather than conceptually representing the ellipse around the points, regression tries to find the single straight line that traces the best path through the points. This is called the line of best fit. The purpose of this, in a very general sense, is that it makes the relationship easier to see. It shows the central tendency of the relationship, so to speak. By that, I mean it shows the most typical value on the $Y$ variable for any given value of $X$. You can just pick any value on the $X$ axis, trace a straight line up to the line of best fit, and then trace a straight line across to the $Y$ axis to find the typical value for that value of $X$. This is in contrast to the correlational idea of tracing an ellipse around the points, which is more akin to showing the dispersion of the points, the variability of the relationship, where regression here shows the central tendency of the relationship.

{{< interactive-figure bestFitLineScatter makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,90],[0.5,60],[0.5,85],[1,65],[1.5,50],[1.5,65],[2,75]],"xLabel":"Coffee (cups)","yLabel":"Test score","xDomain":[0,2.5],"yDomain":[40,100],"line":"fit","controls":false,"maxWidth":"30rem"}' fallback="The coffee and test score scatterplot with the line of best fit drawn through the points, falling from an intercept of 80 with a slope of −10." >}}

<!-- FIX: "the blue one that I'm telling you" is slide narration; check the color against the figure. The line "mathematically minimizes the prediction error" before squaring has been introduced: a reader may think of the plain sum of the misses, which is zero for many lines. Flag that the squares are coming. "would've" three times; "on aggregate" should be "in aggregate". -->

But how do we know the correct line to draw through the points? You can easily imagine a line that's a bit lower than this one, or a bit higher, or one that's at a steeper angle, or one that's shallower. It's obviously hard to tell just from looking, but each of those lines looks like it might be just as good as the blue one that I'm telling you is the best fit line here. So what makes it the best? The line of best fit is the line that mathematically minimizes the prediction error. When a point isn't exactly on the line, it's either at some distance above or below the line of best fit. We call that a prediction error, as in, if you were predicting what the point would have been based only on the best fit line, you would've been a bit off. There would've been some error. So the best fit line mathematically minimizes the collective prediction error. Any other line would've produced more error, on aggregate.

## The equation of a straight line

<!-- FIX: $\hat{Y} = bX + a$ appears here with the hat, is then discussed as $Y$, and the hat isn't explained until the next section. Introduce the school version with plain $Y$. "how much it changes on $Y$" should be "how much $Y$ changes". -->

So how does regression achieve this? Well, you're probably familiar with a lot of this already from high school math. You probably know this equation for a straight line: $\hat{Y} = bX + a$, although you might know a version of it with different letters. When I learned it in school, we learned $Y = mX + c$. I'm not sure why there are different versions, to be honest. Maybe it's a cultural thing. But they are all quantifying the same thing. $X$ and $Y$ are variables: the scores that we plot on the $X$ and $Y$ axes of the scatterplot respectively. $a$ is the intercept: the value of $Y$ when $X$ is zero. Or put more simply, the value of $Y$ when the line meets the $Y$ axis. $b$ is the slope of the line: how much it changes on $Y$ per unit change in $X$.

### The Celsius–Fahrenheit example

You might also be familiar with this particular example of a straight line equation: the relationship between temperatures on the Celsius scale and on the Fahrenheit scale. Obviously the relationship between these two variables is a perfect correlation. There is no variability that isn't completely shared. You can perfectly predict the value of one from the other with no prediction error at all. And the equation for this relationship is $Y = 1.8X + 32$.

| Celsius | Fahrenheit |
|--:|--:|
| 0 | 32 |
| 10 | 50 |
| 20 | 68 |
| 30 | 86 |
| 40 | 104 |
| 50 | 122 |

: Some Celsius temperatures and their Fahrenheit equivalents. {#tbl-celsius-fahrenheit}

Remember, 32 is the intercept. Zero degrees Celsius, so zero on the $X$ axis, corresponds to 32 Fahrenheit, 32 on the $Y$ axis. And 1.8 is the slope. For an increase of one degree Celsius, Fahrenheit increases by 1.8 degrees.

<!-- FIX: "or vice versa." The equation converts Celsius to Fahrenheit; going back means rearranging it. That matters for real data, where the line predicting $X$ from $Y$ is a different line (for the coffee data its slope is −0.025 cups per point, not 1/−10 = −0.1). Correlation is symmetric; regression isn't. Also three sentences starting "So". -->

So this equation allows you to easily convert values from Celsius to Fahrenheit or vice versa. So if you didn't know what 20 Celsius corresponded to, you multiply 20 by 1.8, getting 36, and add 32, getting 68. So 20 Celsius is 68 Fahrenheit. Knowing the values of $b$ and $a$, the slope and the intercept, we can convert between any values of Fahrenheit and Celsius we like.

::: {#quiz-regression-fahrenheit}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-fahrenheit.qmd >}}
:::

## Predicted values and residuals

The regression line follows the same logic. The only difference is that because we're dealing with statistical relationships, rather than pure mathematical relationships like the one between Fahrenheit and Celsius, we refer to $\hat{Y}$ rather than $Y$. $\hat{Y}$ means that this is a predicted value based on the regression equation rather than an observed value that we saw in our data. It distinguishes those predicted $\hat{Y}$ values from the actual $Y$ values that we recorded for that variable.

So this allows us to think about another quantity, $Y - \hat{Y}$. This is called a residual, but it's the same idea as something you're already very familiar with. Remember, a deviation score is $X - M$. Residuals are basically deviations in the context of regression. $Y - \hat{Y}$ quantifies how much each point deviates from the regression line, or the amount of error between the observed value and the predicted value.

<!-- FIX: "least squared error solution": the usual name is "least squares", worth giving since readers will meet "ordinary least squares". -->

And remember how we squared deviations in the past to find sums of squared deviations? Well, we do basically the same thing here. Again, the regression defines the line of best fit. And specifically, that is the line that minimizes the sum of squared residuals. The notation for the sum of squared residuals is $\Sigma(Y - \hat{Y})^2$. So you can see how this is fundamentally the same equation we learned all those chapters ago for the sum of squared deviations. Here in the context of regression, this is called the least squared error solution: the line that results in the lowest possible sum of squared errors.

You can see the least squared error solution in action below. Step through to watch the residuals become literal squares, and then see what happens to them when we swap the best-fit line for a lazier guess.

<!-- PLAN: guess before reveal. Open the controls first ("get the squares as small as you can"), then show the best-fit line. Step copy below is a draft. -->

::::: {#act-least-squares .callout-tip .interactive .with-controls}
## Why is the best-fit line the best?

{{< interactive-figure leastSquaresTutorial makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,90],[0.5,60],[0.5,85],[1,65],[1.5,50],[1.5,65],[2,75]],"xLabel":"Coffee (cups)","yLabel":"Test score","xDomain":[0,2.5],"yDomain":[40,100],"showLine":false,"maxWidth":"30rem"}' fallback="Scatterplot of the coffee and test score data used to demonstrate the least squared error solution: the best-fit line's squared residuals sum to 900, while a flat line at the mean of Y produces squared residuals summing to 1200." >}}

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="The data" data-action='{"line":"none","show-residuals":false,"show-squares":false,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"emphasize":"none","controls-open":false,"animate":false}'}

The line of best fit traces the best path through the points: $\hat{Y} = -10X + 80$.

::: {.tutorial-step data-title="Residuals" data-action='{"line":"fit","show-residuals":true,"show-squares":false,"show-ss":false,"show-means":false,"emphasize":["residuals","points"]}'}

Back to the best-fit line and back to 900. No other line does better---that's what makes it the least squared error solution. Don't take my word for it: the controls are now open, so try any slope and intercept you like.

## Calculating the slope and intercept

### The slope ($b$)

<!-- FIX: "for a unit variation in $X$, how much variation to expect in $Y$" should be "change". "For this data": the book is mixed on "data is/are". Worth adding $b = r \, s_Y / s_X$ here, and from it regression to the mean and where the name comes from. -->

So let's calculate $b$ and $a$ for this little set of data. We find the slope, $b$, by dividing $SP$, the sum of products, which as you remember quantifies the covariability between $X$ and $Y$, by the sum of squares for $X$: $b = \frac{SP}{SS_X}$. This tells us for a unit variation in $X$, how much variation to expect in $Y$. For this data, we calculated $SP$ and $SS_X$ in the previous chapter. We got $-30$ over 3 for an answer of $-10$. In other words, as you move one unit along the $X$ axis, you move down ten units on the $Y$ axis. Going from one to two on the $X$ axis, for example, if you follow the regression line along, the predicted $Y$ value moves from 70 to 60. So the change of one on $X$ corresponds to a change of $-10$ on $Y$.

### The intercept ($a$)

<!-- FIX: this explanation was hard to follow and was written for a positive slope ("reduces $Y$ by that amount"); with $b = -10$, subtracting $b \times M_X$ raises it. Simpler: start at the point of means (1, 70) and walk back one cup to $X = 0$, gaining ten points: 80. Also worth saying what 80 means: the predicted score for a student who drank no coffee (student A, who scored 90). And the extrapolation caution: the same line predicts 40 for four cups and 0 for eight. -->

With $a$, we're determining the intercept of the line---where it crosses the $Y$ axis when $X$ equals zero. To figure this out, we leverage the fact that the best fit line, by definition, will always pass through the point where the mean of $X$ and the mean of $Y$ intersect. Given that the line itself is representing the central tendency of the relationship between $X$ and $Y$, it's only natural that it should pass through the point that reflects their two averages. So $a = M_Y - b \cdot M_X$. $b$ times the mean of $X$ tells us how many units on the $Y$ variable the line will have moved by the time it reaches zero, since it's that many units from zero on the $X$ axis. Subtracting that from the mean of variable $Y$ reduces $Y$ by that amount, revealing the intercept of the line. So here, that's $70 - (-10 \times 1)$, giving 80. So, again, that's the point at which the line intercepts the $Y$ axis: where $X$ equals zero, $Y$ equals 80.

## The standard error of the estimate

So now we have the equation to calculate our $\hat{Y}$ values. We can calculate the prediction error, the deviation of each point from the best fit line. And with that, we can square those residual deviations and sum the squares to find the sum of squared residuals, $SS_{residual}$. Again, notice that this is the exact same process that we've used all along to calculate sums of squared deviations. We're just using slightly different terminology here to talk about the residuals.

| Coffee ($X$) | Test score ($Y$) | $\hat{Y}$ | $Y - \hat{Y}$ | $(Y - \hat{Y})^2$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 90 | 80 | $10$ | 100 |
| 0.5 | 60 | 75 | $-15$ | 225 |
| 0.5 | 85 | 75 | $10$ | 100 |
| 1 | 65 | 70 | $-5$ | 25 |
| 1.5 | 50 | 65 | $-15$ | 225 |
| 1.5 | 65 | 65 | $0$ | 0 |
| 2 | 75 | 60 | $15$ | 225 |

: Predicted values and residuals for the coffee data. {#tbl-residuals}

$$SS_{residual} = \Sigma(Y - \hat{Y})^2 = 100 + 225 + 100 + 25 + 225 + 0 + 225 = 900$$

Here's what those calculations look like on the scatterplot---each labeled point's residual segment and square matches its row in the table:

{{< interactive-figure residualsScatter makeScatterplot options='{"points":[[0,90],[0.5,60],[0.5,85],[1,65],[1.5,50],[1.5,65],[2,75]],"labels":["A","B","C","D","E","F","G"],"pointLabels":true,"xLabel":"Coffee (cups)","yLabel":"Test score","xDomain":[0,2.5],"yDomain":[40,100],"line":"fit","showResiduals":true,"showSquares":true,"showSS":true,"controls":false,"maxWidth":"30rem"}' fallback="The coffee and test score scatterplot with the regression line, each point's residual drawn as a vertical segment to the line, and each squared residual drawn as a literal square; the squares sum to 900." >}}

Do you remember what the square root of sum of squares divided by degrees of freedom is?

::: {#quiz-regression-ss-df}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-ss-df.qmd >}}
:::

<!-- FIX: "If you remember ... well done!" worked as a lecture pause; with the quiz in between it is redundant. The standard error of the estimate has no symbol and no displayed formula (the learning check calls it "s-error"), and nothing says why $df = n - 2$ here when the standard deviation used $n - 1$: the mean cost one, the line costs two (slope and intercept). -->

If you remember that the square root of sum of squares over degrees of freedom gives the standard deviation of a sample of scores, well done! So now I'm going to tell you about another seemingly new concept. But you'll realize it's not really new. It's just another variation on something else you already know about.

In the context of regression, we talk about the standard error of the estimate. The $\hat{Y}$ values that make up the line of best fit give our best guess at $Y$ for any value of $X$. The standard error of the estimate quantifies the precision of the estimate. Or put another way, how much the actual scores tended to vary around those predictions. And if you think about it, this is exactly what standard deviation does. We calculate the mean of a set of scores, and standard deviation quantifies how much points tended to vary around that mean. So the name "standard error of the estimate" for regression here is just another way of saying the standard deviation of points around the line of best fit.

And the concepts are mathematically identical as well. Remember that standard deviation $s$ (or $SD$) was found by taking the square root of the sum of squared deviations over degrees of freedom. The standard error of the estimate is the same: the square root of the sum of squared residuals over the degrees of freedom. Here that's equal to the square root of 900 over $7 - 2$, giving 13.42.

## Partitioning variability

<!-- PLAN: tie this to Chapter 14 in its own terms. $SS_Y$ is $SS_{total}$; the flat line at $M_Y$ is the null model; $SS_{regression}$ plays the part of between groups and $SS_{residual}$ of within. -->

So that's the basic structure of how regression defines the line of best fit and quantifies its prediction error. To complete a regression hypothesis test, though, we're going to go a little further and partition the variability and calculate another sum of squares and degrees of freedom: $SS_{regression}$ and $df_{regression}$.

Notice how we've mostly been framing everything around the $Y$ variable: $\hat{Y}$, the predicted values of $Y$, and $Y - \hat{Y}$, the residuals, the prediction error when we're trying to predict $Y$. So here, to partition the variability, we start with the total variability in $Y$, the sum of squares for $Y$, and we partition that into two components: the sum of squares regression, the variability that the regression model allows us to predict, and the sum of squares residual, the other, unpredictable variability.

{{< interactive-figure regressionPartitionDiagram makeVariancePartitionDiagram options='{"preset":"regression","maxWidth":"38rem"}' fallback="Diagram partitioning the total variability in Y into predictable variability (sum of squares regression) and unpredictable variability (sum of squares residual), whose mean squares form the F ratio for the analysis of regression." >}}

<!-- FIX: $SS_{regression}$ is found by subtraction only. The book defines first: $SS_{regression} = \Sigma(\hat{Y} - M_Y)^2$, how far the line's predictions are from the flat line. For the coffee data: 100 + 25 + 25 + 0 + 25 + 25 + 100 = 300, which matches 1200 − 900. -->

We've just seen how to calculate $SS_{residual}$. And we calculated the sum of squared deviations for $Y$ in the previous chapter, using the usual technique for sums of squares. So we already know those values. The sum of squares regression is just whatever is left over from $SS_Y - SS_{residual}$. Remember, that's because we're partitioning the variability in $Y$ into these two components. So $SS_{regression} + SS_{residual} = SS_Y$. And correspondingly, $SS_Y - SS_{residual} = SS_{regression}$.

<!-- FIX: "$df_{regression}$ is the number of variables minus one" is true but opaque. "One, for the one predictor" is clearer and carries over to two predictors. -->

For the degrees of freedom, $df_Y$ is the number of $Y$ scores minus one. $df_{regression}$ is the number of variables minus one. So with two variables, that equals one. And $df_{residual}$ is $df_Y - df_{regression}$, so $n - 2$. Once we have those sums of squares and degrees of freedom, we do what we usually do with sums of squares and degrees of freedom: we divide them to find a kind of variance, or mean square. Here we find $MS_{regression}$ and $MS_{residual}$. And those become the numerator and denominator of a new $F$ ratio for the regression. This is what we'll use for the hypothesis test. So this technique is known as analysis of regression. And this relies on the same logic of partitioning variance that we learned about with ANOVA.

## A regression test, step by step

### Step 1: State the hypotheses

<!-- FIX: one long paragraph. Worth noting that this is the same null as $\rho = 0$ in Chapter 17. -->

As with any hypothesis test, we need to articulate our hypotheses, and as always, we have a null and an alternative hypothesis. The null here is that the slope of the regression line is zero, which would mean that there is no association between the two variables. Or put another way, it would mean that knowing someone's score on the $X$ variable would not help us predict their score on the $Y$ variable with any more accuracy than just guessing that everyone would score the mean of $Y$. That's what a flat line with a slope of zero indicates: that our best guess at anyone's $Y$ score is just the mean of $Y$, regardless of their score on $X$. (That's exactly the flat line we pitted against the best-fit line in the interactive earlier---the one whose squared error came out to $SS_Y$.) The alternative hypothesis is that the slope is not equal to zero. And notice that the slope that we calculated based on our sample is labeled $b$. But the population parameter we're interested in with our hypotheses here is labeled with the Greek symbol $\beta$. This is the usual logic that we don't really care about our sample itself, only about what inferences it helps us make about the population, which is what we're really interested in.

$$ H_0: \beta = 0 $$

$$ H_1: \beta \ne 0 $$

### Step 2: Set the decision criteria

Step two is to find the critical value for the test statistic. And since we're using an $F$ ratio, we use the $F$ table. The degrees of freedom for the numerator, $df_{regression}$, is one here. And for the denominator, $df_{residual}$ is $7 - 2$, which is five. With $\alpha = .05$, the critical value is 6.61. We reject the null if $F > 6.61$.

::: {#tbl-regression-critical}
{{< interactive-figure regressionCriticalTable makeFTable options='{"title":"Critical values for the coffee test","alpha":0.05,"df1":{"from":1,"to":4},"df2":{"from":3,"to":7},"tableMinWidth":"0","maxWidth":"32rem","interactive":false,"selected":{"df1":1,"df2":5,"alpha":0.05}}' fallback="F table excerpt for numerator df 1 through 4 and denominator df 3 through 7, highlighting the .05 critical value of 6.61 at F(1, 5)." >}}

An excerpt of the $F$ table for $\alpha = .05$, with the critical value for $F(1, 5)$ highlighted.
:::

### Step 3: Collect and analyze the data

Step three is to calculate the $F$ ratio for the data. Some of the required values we already calculated earlier in this chapter or in the previous chapter. So whether you already have them noted down, or you need to recalculate them, see if you can get all the required sums of squares and degrees of freedom to calculate the numerator and denominator of the test statistic and find the $F$ ratio.

::: {#quiz-regression-calculate-f}
{{< include quizzes/18-regression-calculate-f.qmd >}}
:::

Here's the full working, so you can check your answers:

::: {#tbl-regression-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Regression | 300 | 1 | 300 | 1.67 |
| Residual | 900 | 5 | 180 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1200 | 6 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Summary table for the analysis of regression on the coffee data.
:::

$$
MS_{regression} = \frac{300}{1} = 300 \qquad
MS_{residual} = \frac{900}{5} = 180 \qquad
F = \frac{300}{180} = 1.67
$$

### Step 4: Make a decision

With our $F$ ratio in hand, we next make our decision. If $F$ is greater than the critical value, we can reject the null hypothesis. Our $F$ of 1.67 falls short of the critical value of 6.61 for $F(1, 5)$ at $\alpha = .05$. Here, as with the correlation for this data in the previous chapter, we fail to reject the null. The sample size is just too small for this kind of test to come out as significant. So it's not possible to say that the data is sufficiently unlikely that we can reject our null hypothesis of no association.

::: {#fig-regression-decision}
{{< interactive-figure regressionTestDecision makeDistributionGraph options='{"color":"var(--sfs-null-color, currentColor)","distribution":"f","df1":1,"df2":5,"title":"Null distribution: F(1, 5)","style":"minimal","xAxis":true,"yLabel":false,"xDomain":[0,10],"yDomain":[0,1.6],"points":160,"xTicks":6,"labels":{"x":"F ratio"},"shade":{"tail":"right","alpha":0.05},"markers":[{"at":6.607891,"label":"6.61","height":0.45,"color":"var(--sfs-critical-color, #c63f3f)"},{"at":1.666667,"label":"F = 1.67","height":0.6,"color":"var(--sfs-accent, #2c7fb8)"}],"maxWidth":"42rem"}' fallback="Null F distribution with 1 and 5 degrees of freedom. The rejection region lies beyond 6.61; the observed F of 1.67 falls short of it." >}}

The observed $F = 1.67$ falls short of the critical value of the null $F$ distribution with 1 and 5 degrees of freedom.
:::

<!-- PLAN: exact p = .25, the same as for the correlation in Chapter 17, because it is the same test: F = 1.67 = (−1.29)², and the critical value 6.61 = 2.571². See "One test, three ways" below. -->

### Step 5: Estimate the effect, interval, and power

#### Effect size: $r^2$

<!-- FIX: "for completeness, I need to mention" undersells the most useful number in the chapter. Say that $r^2 = SS_{regression}/SS_Y$ is the same ratio as $\eta^2 = SS_{between}/SS_{total}$ in Chapter 14. -->

Usually this means we wouldn't need to know the effect size because we can't be sure that there is a real effect. But for completeness, I need to mention that our measure of effect size here would be $r^2$. Given the close conceptual links between regression and correlation, it should make some kind of sense that we can square the correlation coefficient as a measure of effect size here. Specifically in this context, we call it the coefficient of determination.

$$r^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_Y} = \frac{300}{1200} = .25$$

But despite the new name, it quantifies essentially the same thing I said when we first introduced the idea of $r^2$: the proportion of variability in the data that we can attribute to the relationship between our variables.

<!-- FIX: this paragraph contradicts Chapter 17. "Saying one variable caused the difference in another is just another way of saying that the variable was related" is the claim that chapter argues against: what licenses "cause" is random assignment, whatever statistic follows. If the philosophical point is wanted, it could be attributed (Pearson held that causation was only the limiting case of correlation) and then answered. -->

The only difference is that previously, in the context of the $t$ test, we talked about the independent variable causing a difference on the dependent variable. Here we talk about changes in one variable being associated with changes in another. But philosophically speaking, saying one variable caused the difference in another is just another way of saying that the variable was related to changes in the other variable.

<!-- PLAN: #### Confidence interval. For the slope, 95% CI is about [−29.9, 9.9] points per cup ($s_b = \sqrt{MS_{residual}/SS_X} = 7.75$). -->

<!-- PLAN: #### Statistical power. Same as for the correlation in Chapter 17. -->

## Reporting and interpreting the results

### Reporting results

<!-- FIX: "$b = -10$" needs units to mean anything: ten points lower per extra cup. Chapter 17 reports the exact $p$ (.25); this says only "$p > .05$", matching the paragraph above it. -->

So finally, we can report the results. Here, we can mention the general trend in the data as quantified in $b$, the slope of the regression line. And then we mention the $F$ ratio for the analysis of regression with its degrees of freedom, whether $p$ was less than or greater than $\alpha$, and, if it was significant, the effect size.

> Drinking more coffee was associated with lower test performance, $b = -10$. However, the association was nonsignificant; $F(1, 5) = 1.67$, $p > .05$.

### Interpreting the results

<!-- PLAN: new. (1) Failing to reject, as in Chapter 17. (2) Prediction is not causation: "predict", "explained" and "predictable variability" all sound causal, but prediction runs happily in the non-causal direction (test score "predicts" that morning's coffee just as well). (3) Extrapolation: the line is only good for the range of the data. (4) Assumptions: linearity, independent observations, residuals roughly normal with similar spread all along the line (the regression counterpart of homogeneity of variance). -->

## Adding a second predictor

<!-- PLAN (2026-11-16): new section; nothing here is Rob's prose yet. Tables, equations and numbers are live; the explanation is sketched in DRAFT comments. It picks up Chapter 17's third variable: the same seven students, with their sleep. Whether the formulas for the two slopes belong in the text or a footnote is open. -->

<!-- DRAFT: In Chapter 17 we asked whether sleep might account for the association between coffee and test scores, and found that the partial correlation for our seven students was −.10, down from −.50. Regression can ask the same question by using both variables as predictors at once. This is multiple regression, and it is what makes regression an extension of correlation. -->

| Participant | Coffee ($X$) | Sleep ($Z$) | Test score ($Y$) |
|:--:|:--:|:--:|:--:|
| A | 0 | 9 | 90 |
| B | 0.5 | 8 | 60 |
| C | 0.5 | 8 | 85 |
| D | 1 | 5 | 65 |
| E | 1.5 | 6 | 50 |
| F | 1.5 | 6 | 65 |
| G | 2 | 7 | 75 |

: The seven students' coffee, sleep, and test scores, from Chapter 17. {#tbl-coffee-sleep-scores-again}

<!-- DRAFT: The equation gains a term. Each predictor gets its own slope, and there is still one intercept. Each slope now says how much $Y$ changes per unit of that predictor while the other predictor is held constant. -->

$$ \hat{Y} = b_1 X + b_2 Z + a $$ {#eq-multiple-regression}

<!-- DRAFT: The slopes come from the same ingredients as before, sums of squares and sums of products, now including the ones involving sleep: $SS_Z = 12$, $SP_{XZ} = -4$, $SP_{ZY} = 80$. -->

$$ b_1 = \frac{SP_{XY}\,SS_Z - SP_{XZ}\,SP_{ZY}}{SS_X\,SS_Z - SP_{XZ}^2} = \frac{(-30)(12) - (-4)(80)}{(3)(12) - (-4)^2} = \frac{-40}{20} = -2 $$

$$ b_2 = \frac{SP_{ZY}\,SS_X - SP_{XZ}\,SP_{XY}}{SS_X\,SS_Z - SP_{XZ}^2} = \frac{(80)(3) - (-4)(-30)}{(3)(12) - (-4)^2} = \frac{120}{20} = 6 $$

$$ a = M_Y - b_1 M_X - b_2 M_Z = 70 - (-2)(1) - (6)(7) = 30 $$

$$ \hat{Y} = -2X + 6Z + 30 $$

<!-- DRAFT: With coffee alone, each extra cup went with a score 10 points lower. With sleep in the equation, each extra cup goes with a score only 2 points lower, among students who slept the same amount. Each extra hour of sleep goes with a score 6 points higher, among students who drank the same amount of coffee. Same story as the partial correlation. -->

| Coffee ($X$) | Sleep ($Z$) | Score ($Y$) | $\hat{Y}$ | $Y - \hat{Y}$ | $(Y - \hat{Y})^2$ |
|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| 0 | 9 | 90 | 84 | $6$ | 36 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 60 | 77 | $-17$ | 289 |
| 0.5 | 8 | 85 | 77 | $8$ | 64 |
| 1 | 5 | 65 | 58 | $7$ | 49 |
| 1.5 | 6 | 50 | 63 | $-13$ | 169 |
| 1.5 | 6 | 65 | 63 | $2$ | 4 |
| 2 | 7 | 75 | 68 | $7$ | 49 |

: Predicted values and residuals with both coffee and sleep as predictors. $SS_{residual} = 660$. {#tbl-multiple-residuals}

<!-- DRAFT: The partition works exactly as before. $SS_Y$ is still 1200. The residual is now 660, so the regression accounts for 540. There are two predictors, so $df_{regression} = 2$, and $df_{residual} = n - 3 = 4$: the equation now pins down three things. -->

::: {#tbl-multiple-regression-summary .sfs-summary-table}
| Source | $SS$ | $df$ | $MS$ | $F$ |
|:-------|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| Regression | 540 | 2 | 270 | 1.64 |
| Residual | 660 | 4 | 165 | []{.sfs-na} |
| Total | 1200 | 6 | []{.sfs-na} | []{.sfs-na} |

Summary table for the regression with coffee and sleep as predictors.
:::

$$ R^2 = \frac{SS_{regression}}{SS_Y} = \frac{540}{1200} = .45 $$

<!-- DRAFT: The critical value for $F(2, 4)$ is 6.94, so this is nonsignificant too ($p = .30$): seven students again. The two predictors together account for 45% of the variability in test scores, against 25% for coffee alone. Sleep alone accounts for 44% ($r_{ZY}^2 = .667^2$), so adding coffee to sleep adds almost nothing. Capital $R^2$ is the convention with more than one predictor. Cautions: same as Chapter 17 (only measured variables are accounted for; not an experiment). A test for each slope separately exists and is beyond this book. -->

## One test, three ways

<!-- PLAN: a possible closing section, using only numbers already in the book.

| | Statistic | df | p |
| Ch 17: correlation | t = −1.29 | 5 | .25 |
| Ch 18: regression | F = 1.67 = (−1.29)² | 1, 5 | .25 |

Critical values: 2.571² = 6.61. This is Chapter 14's F = t² again. Add the point-biserial result (Chapter 12's t is a correlation with a 0/1 variable, and the slope of that regression is the difference between the group means) and the reader has the t test, ANOVA, correlation and regression as one family: the general linear model without the name. Also: $SS_{regression} = r^2 \times SS_Y$ and $SS_{residual} = (1 - r^2) \times SS_Y$, which is where Chapter 17's standard error $\sqrt{(1 - r^2)/(n - 2)}$ came from. -->
